summary: OOPMAS has a GPT-5 meta-agent write object-oriented agent classes and a per-query Python main() workflow, then re-run and repair that workflow for R rounds (5 on Mixed, 3 on Hard Mixed) using a task scorer and a run-local skill library. On a 120-query Mixed set (HumanEval, MBPP, MATH, GSM8K, HotpotQA, DROP) and a 180-query Hard Mixed set (AIME, LiveCodeBench/CodeContests, GPQA Diamond), it reports 89.6% and 90.8% against 71.5% and 72.3% for ADAS. The optimisation loop scores each reported query with its own ground-truth evaluator. The headline is therefore oracle-guided per-query retry, not the accuracy of a deployable workflow generator.

claims.claim: OOPMAS beats the best task-level MAS-generation baseline by +18.1 points on Mixed (89.6 vs 71.5 ADAS).
claims.evidence: Table 1 shows the numbers. But Algorithm 1 (lines 10-15) computes Score(W, q_i) on the reported query each round and triggers Diagnose&Fix on 'wrong output', which needs the label. The reported figure is also 'the highest score across the two configurations' (skill library on/off, §4.1). All queries are 'drawn from the validation splits', with no held-out test split. Baselines are not given per-query label feedback.

claims.claim: The gap holds on Hard Mixed (90.8 vs 72.3, +18.5), 'showing that per-query generation generalises rather than relying on benchmark-specific memorisation'.
claims.evidence: Hard Mixed uses the same in-loop oracle scoring. The ADAS Hard Mixed row has no per-domain cells and MaAS has none at all. OOPMAS reports 98.3% on GPQA Diamond and 98.3% on AIME with GPT-5, which is consistent with repeated retries against the answer key rather than first-attempt accuracy. A stable gap between two oracle-advantaged runs does not test memorisation versus generalisation.

claims.claim: Fixed task-level workflows collapse on heterogeneous mixed streams (AFlow 90/0/0 on code/math/QA).
claims.evidence: Table 1 shows AFlow at 0.0 on math and QA and 0.0 on Hard code, which the authors attribute to output-format mismatch. That reads as a misconfigured baseline: one AFlow workflow was searched on one domain and applied to all. No per-domain router or format adapter was tried, so it measures a format failure, not a structural limit of static workflows.

claims.claim: OOPMAS scales with model capability, reaching 92.4% with GPT-5.2.
claims.evidence: Figure 4 shows 72.5 to 92.4 from GPT-4.1 to GPT-5.2. At GPT-5-nano, AFlow's fixed scaffold scores 65.4 and OOPMAS 51.0, so the static workflow wins with a weak model (also in Limitations). Single runs per model.

claims.claim: The agent pool and per-query generation drive accuracy; the skill library adds marginal points.
claims.evidence: Fig. 3: every ablation stays within ±3.5 points of Full. Full is the median of 4 seeds while Table 1 is a single best-of-two-configs run. No ablation removes the in-loop Score feedback, which is the most likely driver. Appendix B says 'most queries terminate within a single agent call', so the multi-agent structure is mostly unused.

patterns.note: The meta-agent emits a per-query executable workflow (Python main() over agent objects), the LLM-generated-workflow form of P37. Comparison: same worker model (GPT-5) against ADAS, MetaAgent, MaAS and AFlow, but OOPMAS alone gets R rounds of per-query ground-truth Score feedback, and two baselines collapse to 0 on whole domains (strawman). There is no plain GPT-5 baseline and no plain GPT-5 + same-budget retry-with-tests baseline. Counter-evidence: at GPT-5-nano the fixed AFlow workflow beats generation 65.4 vs 51.0, and App. B says most queries finish in one agent call, so the generated DAG structure is rarely exercised. Not an isolating test of generated DAGs.

AFlow's single searched workflow is the static-workflow stand-in. It collapses on mixed streams through output-format mismatch (0 on math/QA) but beats OOPMAS with a weak model (GPT-5-nano 65.4 vs 51.0). No static workflow with a per-domain router or format adapter was tried, so the paper does not show static graphs failing when configured reasonably.

Per-query search and repair with a run-local skill library. Its gains are confounded with ground-truth feedback on the reported queries, and ablating the skill library moves accuracy by at most 3.5 points.
Framed as multi-agent generation, but App. B says most queries terminate within a single agent call, and no single-agent baseline is reported.
The repair loop is driven by the task's own evaluator (unit tests, answer match) on the evaluated query: execution feedback used as an oracle, not as a verifier available at deployment.
Reports a ~7x (Mixed, $35 vs $15) and ~11x (Hard, $271 vs $25) cost premium over ADAS. Baseline costs are estimates, not measured (Fig. 5 caption).

methodology.sample: 120 Mixed queries (40 code, 40 math, 40 QA) from benchmark validation splits; 180 Hard Mixed queries (AIME 2025/26, LiveCodeBench, CodeContests, GPQA Diamond).
methodology.baselines: ADAS, MetaAgent, MaAS, AFlow, all with GPT-5. AFlow scores 0 on whole domains and MaAS has missing cells. Hard ADAS has no per-domain numbers. No plain-model, CoT or self-consistency baseline, and no baseline with the same per-query test feedback.
methodology.models: GPT-5 as meta-agent and worker; model swap with GPT-4.1, GPT-5-nano, GPT-5.2 (Mixed only).
methodology.variance: Main table is a single run, reporting the best of two configurations. Ablation 'Full' is the median of 4 seeds. No CIs.
methodology.ablations: Component ablation (memory, skill create/update/select, coverage check), all within ±3.5 points. No ablation of in-loop Score feedback or of multi-agent structure.
methodology.contamination_controls: None. The evaluator's label is consumed inside the optimisation loop on the reported queries. Public benchmarks with known contamination risk (HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K).
methodology.languages: Python code tasks (function completion, stdin/stdout); math; English QA.

standards.artifacts: No code or data link. The text refers to a codebase producing cost_summary.json, but no URL is given.

biases.detail: Score(W, q_i) on the reported query drives Diagnose&Fix for R rounds (Alg. 1), so reported accuracy is closer to pass@R-with-oracle than to first-shot accuracy.
AFlow is applied as a single-domain workflow to a mixed stream and scores 0 on math and QA. No reasonable static baseline (per-domain router, plain GPT-5, retry-with-tests at matched budget).
The headline reports the higher of two OOPMAS configurations (skill library on/off).
Single run for Table 1 and the model swap; only the ablation 'Full' uses a 4-seed median.
The authors built both the Mixed/Hard Mixed benchmarks and the top system, scored with their own pipeline.
Public benchmark items (HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH, GPQA) with no contamination check.
Baseline costs are estimated from configurations, not measured.
No code or data link in the paper.

coi.affiliations: Rutgers University, University of Pittsburgh, University of Maryland, NEC Laboratories America.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None. All models are OpenAI. NEC sells no product evaluated here.
coi.detail: No vendor self-grading. The authors construct both the benchmarks and the winning method, which is the main independence concern.

verdict_reason: The headline comparison is confounded by design. OOPMAS optimises each workflow against the ground-truth scorer of the very query it reports, while baselines do not get that feedback, and the reported number is the better of two configurations on validation-split items with no held-out test. Two of four baselines are degenerate (0 on whole domains) and no plain-model or matched-retry baseline exists. The remaining evidence (ablation within ±3.5, most queries using one agent call, a fixed workflow winning at GPT-5-nano) does not isolate the claimed mechanism.
applicability: For the Java multi-repo team's DAG question this paper gives no usable evidence that LLM-generated per-task workflows beat a fixed workflow. Its gains come from retrying against the answer key, which a team cannot do on real ingestion changes, though it can do something similar against its own build and tests. The transferable observations cut the other way. A fixed workflow is more robust with weaker or cheaper models (AFlow beats generation at GPT-5-nano). Generated workflows cost roughly 7-11x more. Most generated 'multi-agent' workflows collapse to a single call. If the team trials generated plans, compare them against a plain agent with the same test-and-retry budget on Java tasks, not against a mis-scoped static pipeline.

conflicts_with.detail: Same author group. RA-MoWE reports that its deployable text-routed workflow bank does not beat Direct prompting significantly and ties single-call CoT. That undercuts OOPMAS's implication that query-level workflow generation yields large gains on similar mixed math/code/QA streams once oracle feedback is removed.

OpenCollab finds model-directed multi-agent organisations often do not run as declared, and that gains come from a code-scripted fixed workflow (Duo) at the same model. OOPMAS argues fixed workflows fail on mixed streams, but its fixed baseline is mis-scoped.

Harness-tampering work shows self-improving harnesses that touch their own evaluation channel inflate gains. OOPMAS feeds the evaluator's label into its own per-query optimisation, the evaluation-channel coupling that paper warns about.
